Why: Chapter one. Why markets underinsure, and what the state can pool.

Insurance works by pooling. On the Island, each worker has a three percent chance of losing their job in a normal year, and nine percent in a recession, which comes one year in seven. If job losses were independent, an insurer with ten thousand members would know almost exactly what it would pay: the spread of the claim per member falls with the square root of the pool, to 5 percent of the average at ten thousand. But unemployment comes in waves. In a recession everyone's risk rises at once, and no pool, however large, brings the spread below 55 percent of the average. A private insurer would need enormous reserves for the bad years. A government can do what a company cannot: borrow in the recession and repay in the boom, spreading the risk across years and generations.

Kenneth Arrow's 1963 article on medical care began the study of why insurance markets fail. There are four main reasons. Adverse selection: those who know they are risky buy the most insurance, prices rise, and the safe drop out, which Part thirteen showed can unravel a market. Moral hazard: the insured take less care, or search less hard for work. Common shocks: recessions and pandemics hit everyone at once. And risks that are settled before anyone can buy cover: no one can insure, before birth, against the family or the health they will be born with. The state has tools no company has. It can make everyone join, which ends adverse selection. It can borrow across the cycle. And through taxes and transfers it can insure people against the luck of the draw, as if the contract had been signed before anyone knew their lot.

America's unemployment insurance is run by the states. How much of the risk does it actually cover? Divide the number claiming state benefits each week by the number of unemployed counted by the household survey. Since 1967 the share has averaged 35 percent. In 2019, a year of low unemployment, it was 28 percent. In 2020, when the pandemic closed whole industries at once, it rose to 72 percent. In 2026 it is 25 percent. Most of the unemployed draw nothing: they did not work long enough to qualify, they quit, their benefits ran out, or they never applied. How generous benefits should be, for those who get them, is the next question.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: set the unemployment benefit.

Your turn. On the Island, workers who lose their jobs look for new ones. The harder they search, the likelier they are to find work, but searching is costly. If the search fails, they receive a benefit, a share of the wage. If it succeeds, they earn the wage, less a tax that pays for everyone's benefits. They also have savings and a partner's income to fall back on, and they dislike risk about as much as the typical estimate. Which benefit makes them best off, counting both the comfort it gives and the search it discourages: a tenth of the wage, a third, a half, or three quarters? Pause, and choose.

The answer is B, about a third. At that benefit, 84 percent of those who lose their jobs find work within the period, the tax that pays for the benefits is 6.5 percent of the wage, and consumption falls by 15 percent on losing the job. Less generous, and the unemployed bear too much of the risk. More generous, and too many stop looking, so that the tax to pay for it all rises faster than the comfort it buys.

Here is the whole trade. Expected welfare, counting the comfort of benefits and the cost of searching, rises with the benefit at first, then falls. Behind it, two forces. As benefits rise, the chance of finding work within the period falls, because the unemployed search less. And the fall in consumption on losing a job shrinks, which is what insurance is for. The top is at 33 percent of the wage. The next chapter finds the same answer from a formula that needs only two numbers, both of which can be measured.
Baily: Chapter three. Optimal unemployment insurance, derived.

Martin Baily in 1978, and Raj Chetty in 2006, reduced the question to a formula. Take one worker who has lost a job. Welfare is the chance e of finding work times the utility of consumption when employed, plus the chance of not finding it times the utility when unemployed, minus the cost of searching. The benefits are paid by a tax on those who find work, so the budget balances. Raise the benefit a little. The unemployed gain the marginal utility of their consumption on each extra dollar; the employed lose it on the extra tax. The worker's own change in search does not count, because it was already chosen to make the worker best off. The tax must rise for two reasons: to pay the higher benefit, and because fewer people now find work and pay in. Set the change in welfare to zero, and out comes Baily's formula. On the left, how much more a dollar is worth to the unemployed than to the employed. On the right, the elasticity of the chance of staying unemployed with respect to the benefit, divided by the chance of finding work: the cost of the extra unemployment benefits cause.

On the Island, both sides can be computed at every benefit. The gain from smoothing consumption is large when benefits are small, because losing a job then means a deep fall in consumption, and it shrinks as benefits rise. The cost rises with the benefit, as more people search less and the tax to pay for them climbs. They cross at 33 percent of the wage, where both equal 0.40. That is exactly the benefit that maximized welfare in the game. The formula is not an approximation in this model; it is the condition for the best benefit, written in quantities that can be measured.

To use the formula on real data, one more step. For moderate falls in consumption, the left side is approximately risk aversion, gamma, times the percentage fall in consumption on losing a job. So the rule becomes: benefits are about right when risk aversion times the consumption drop equals the elasticity of unemployment with respect to benefits. Risk aversion is the subject of Part seven. The consumption drop can be measured in household surveys. And the elasticity can be measured from changes in benefits. The next chapter measures the last two.
Measure: First, the cost side: how much do benefits lengthen unemployment? Watch a worker on the Island, week by week. Benefits pay half the wage for 26 weeks, then only a floor. In the first week the chance of finding a job is 6.3 percent. As the end of benefits approaches, the worker searches harder, and in the last week and after it is 13.4 percent. Bruce Meyer saw this in American data in 1990: the chance of leaving unemployment jumps when benefits are about to lapse. The average spell lasts 12.8 weeks. Raise the benefit by ten percent, and spells lengthen by 3.8 percent: an elasticity of 0.41. Pay benefits for thirty weeks instead of twenty, and 10 percent fewer find work in the first twenty weeks.

In real economies the same numbers have been measured many ways. In America, comparing workers in states and years with different benefits, a ten percent higher benefit lengthens spells by four to eight percent. In Austria, David Card, Raj Chetty and Andrea Weber compared workers just either side of the work record that entitled them to thirty weeks of benefits rather than twenty: job finding in the first twenty weeks was five to nine percent lower. The same design, at three years in a job, the cutoff for severance pay, found that a lump sum of two months' earnings lowered job finding by eight to twelve percent. A lump sum does not reward staying unemployed; that finding matters in chapter five. In Germany, Johannes Schmieder, Till von Wachter and Stefan Bender used the ages at which longer benefits begin, year after year, and found the effects at most somewhat smaller in recessions, when extensions also reach more people.

Now the gain side: how far does consumption fall? In 1997 Jonathan Gruber used food spending in the Panel Study of Income Dynamics: on losing a job, families cut it by about seven percent on average, and without unemployment benefits the fall would have been more than three times as large. Each ten points of replacement made the fall about 2.7 percent smaller. In 2019 Peter Ganong and Pascal Noel used bank accounts, which record all spending month by month: about six percent at the start of unemployment, and then about twelve percent more in the month benefits run out, a larger drop than in all the months before.

Put the numbers in the formula, rearranged to ask what risk aversion would make today's benefits right. With a seven percent drop and an elasticity between 0.4 and 0.8, the answer is a risk aversion of 5.7 to 11.4. That is high: most estimates are lower. Gruber drew the same conclusion: the benefit levels of his time were justified only at fairly high risk aversion. But the drop at exhaustion is larger, about twelve percent, which needs only 3.3 to 6.7. Ganong and Noel concluded that the gains from paying benefits for longer are several times the gains from paying more each week. And there is a deeper objection to the whole calculation, the subject of the next chapter.
Liquidity: Chapter five. Moral hazard or liquidity?

Why do benefits lengthen unemployment? In 2008 Raj Chetty separated two reasons. A higher benefit changes search in two ways. It gives the unemployed more cash, so they need not grab the first job that comes along: the liquidity effect, the same as giving them money whether or not they work. And it narrows the gap between working and not working: moral hazard, a reward for staying unemployed. Only the second is a distortion. The first is the insurance doing its job, letting people who cannot borrow search as they would if they could. Chetty showed that the share of the response due to liquidity, L, fixes the left side of the formula: L over one minus L. On the Island, at its best benefit, a little more benefit lowers the chance of finding work by 0.039 through liquidity and 0.099 through moral hazard: liquidity is 28 percent of the response.

How large is the liquidity share? On the Island it is largest when benefits are small, because then losing a job means a deep fall in consumption, and cash in hand matters most. At the Island's best benefit it is 28 percent. Chetty measured it for American workers in two ways: benefits lengthen spells much more for households with little savings than for those with plenty, and lump-sum severance pay, which rewards no one for staying unemployed, lengthens spells for the cash-poor. Combining the two, about sixty percent of the effect of benefits on durations is liquidity.

What does sixty percent imply? The gain side of the formula becomes 0.6 over 0.4, which is 1.5. That is far above any plausible cost of longer spells, so benefits should rise. Chetty's calculation put the optimal benefit above half of the wage. Notice the tension. Measured through the consumption drop, today's benefits look generous enough; measured through liquidity, they look too low. The two routes rest on different data and different assumptions about how well households can borrow and save, and the disagreement is not settled.
Health: Chapter six. Health insurance and moral hazard.

Kenneth Arrow argued in 1963 that medical care is unlike other goods: illness is uncertain, and doctors know far more than their patients. Insurance protects against the cost of illness, but it also lowers the price of care at the moment of use, so people use more of it, which Mark Pauly called moral hazard. How much more? From the 1970s to 1982 the RAND Corporation ran the largest social experiment of its time: 2,750 families, more than 7,700 people, at six sites. Each family was assigned at random to free care, or to paying a quarter, a half or ninety-five percent of its medical bills, with a cap related to income. Those paying ninety-five percent spent about thirty percent less than those with free care; those paying a quarter, about twenty percent less. And on average their health was not measurably worse, though some of the poorest and sickest did worse with less care.

So insurance has a cost as well as a benefit, and the best plan trades them off, a problem Richard Zeckhauser set out in 1970. On the Island, illnesses of every size strike seven in ten people a year, and care repairs the harm with diminishing returns. The less of each bill a patient pays, the less risk they bear: the purple line falls to zero with free care. But the less they pay, the more care they buy that is worth less than it costs: the gold line rises as coinsurance falls. The white line is the sum. It is lowest when patients pay about 28 percent of each bill. The Island is set so that, as in RAND, patients paying ninety-five percent spend thirty percent less than with free care. Real plans also cap what anyone pays in a year, which removes most of the remaining risk while keeping a price on the first visits.

Four lessons. RAND's response is often summarized as a price elasticity of about minus 0.2. On the Island, between the twenty-five and ninety-five percent plans, it is minus 0.23. But Aliza Aron-Dine, Liran Einav and Amy Finkelstein showed that the summary is fragile: with deductibles and caps there is no single price, and the number depends on which one is used. Patients who paid more cut care that was highly effective in roughly equal proportions to care that did not. That suggests a design: make care of high value cheap, and care of low value dear, instead of one price for everything.
Oregon: How do you learn from a lottery when not every winner takes up the prize? Many people drawn never applied, or did not qualify, and some who were not drawn found coverage elsewhere. On the Island's version of Oregon, 40 percent of those drawn ended up insured, against 14 percent of the rest. The difference, about a quarter, is the first stage, close to Oregon's twenty-five points. The trick is to compare everyone drawn with everyone not drawn, whether or not they were insured, because only that comparison is guaranteed fair. Then divide the gap in outcomes by the gap in coverage. If insurance moves an outcome by some amount, a lottery that raises coverage by a quarter moves it by a quarter as much; dividing by the first stage scales it back up. This is the Wald estimator of Part four, an instrument made by chance.

Here is what Oregon found, in papers led by Amy Finkelstein and Katherine Baicker. Insurance raised the use of care: outpatient visits by about thirty-five percent, prescriptions by about fifteen. Emergency visits rose too, by about forty percent, against the hope that coverage would move people from the emergency room to the doctor's office. It removed financial strain: medical bills above thirty percent of a household's income were virtually eliminated. It reduced depression, by about nine percentage points from thirty, a large effect. But in two years it produced no statistically significant change in measured blood pressure, cholesterol, or blood sugar.

Does that mean insurance does nothing for blood pressure? Not necessarily, and the Island shows why. Plant a true effect of one point of blood pressure, run the lottery two hundred times with twelve thousand people measured each time, and estimate the effect each time. Because only a quarter of those drawn gained coverage, each estimate is noisy: it is statistically significant in only 14 percent of the runs. The smallest effect this design would reliably detect is about 3.2 points; anything smaller would usually go unseen. The same runs detect the planted effect on depression 76 percent of the time. No detectable effect is not the same as no effect: the experiment could rule out large effects, not small ones.

One more question: what is Medicaid worth to the people it covers? Amy Finkelstein, Nathaniel Hendren and Erzo Luttmer used Oregon's results to estimate it. Recipients would pay between fifty cents and a dollar twenty for each dollar their care costs. The reason it is not more is that the uninsured already received much of their care without paying for it, and about sixty cents of each government dollar is, in effect, a transfer to those who had been paying for that care. Before, hospitals, other patients and taxpayers bore that cost through unpaid bills. So Medicaid is partly insurance for them: a transfer to the people who would otherwise have paid. Who benefits from a programme is not always who receives it.
Pensions: Most public pensions are pay-as-you-go: today's workers pay for today's retirees. Part twenty-two showed, after Paul Samuelson, why that can be a good deal. Its arithmetic is simple. If the pension is paid only from contributions, the benefit as a share of the wage equals the contribution rate times the number of workers per retiree. America's Social Security is financed by a payroll tax of 12.4 percent, shared by employer and employee. In 1960 there were 5.1 covered workers per beneficiary: that tax could pay each beneficiary 63 percent of the average wage. Today there are 2.7, enough for 33 percent. By 2035 the trustees project 2.3, enough for 29 percent. The trust fund, built up from past surpluses, fills the gap for now; the trustees expect it to run out in 2034.

What return does a pay-as-you-go pension pay? The growth of the total wage bill: on the Island, with workers growing by half a percent a year and wages by one, about 1.5 percent. A funded account, invested, earns the return on capital, here three percent. Over a thirty-year career a dollar paid in becomes 1 dollar 57 in pay-as-you-go, against 2 dollars 43 in a fund: 36 percent less. So why not switch? Because the first generation of retirees was paid without having contributed, and every later generation was promised the same. That promise is a debt, owed to today's retirees and workers. Paying it off, or paying interest on it, costs exactly the gap in returns. A switch to funding moves the cost between generations; it does not make it disappear.

What can reform do? A later retirement age adds workers and removes retirees, attacking both sides of the ratio. Sweden's reform of the late 1990s kept pay-as-you-go financing but gave each worker a notional account: benefits follow what you paid in, and adjust to how long your generation is expected to live, so longer lives do not break the budget. Building a reserve now, partly pre-funding, lets later workers pay less. America chose a mix of these in 1983, with a promise that chapter fifteen checks.
Defaults: Part seven met Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea's study; here is what it means for policy. On 1 April 1998, a large American firm changed one thing about its retirement plan: new employees were enrolled automatically, unless they asked not to be. Among workers hired the year before, who had to sign up, 37 percent were saving at the same tenure. Among those hired after the switch, 86 percent. The default was three percent of pay, in a money market fund, and 76 percent of the automatically enrolled stayed at exactly that rate, although few had chosen it before. A default is not neutral: it is a decision made for everyone who does not decide.

Why does a default matter so much? Inertia is enough. On the Island, employees get round to choosing a savings plan only occasionally, about once in two years on average, and when they do, three in four choose to save. If they must opt in, 37 percent are saving after fifteen months. Enrolled automatically, 87 percent: close to the firm's numbers. And 56 percent are still at the default rate, not because they chose it but because they have not yet chosen. The gap closes only slowly, as people get round to deciding; meanwhile, the default decides.

Do defaults raise saving, or just move it? Raj Chetty and coauthors followed the savings of Danes in 41 million records. About 85 percent are passive: they do not respond to tax subsidies at all, but they keep whatever an employer or the government saves for them automatically, so automatic contributions raise their total saving. About 15 percent are active, and respond to a subsidy mostly by moving money from one account to another. So each dollar of subsidy raised total saving by about one cent. Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow uses inertia the other way: employees commit now to save part of future raises, and in the first firm to try it, saving rates rose from 3.5 percent to 13.6 percent in 40 months, among those who chose to join.
Disability: Disability insurance replaces the earnings of people who can no longer work. Its difficulty is screening. An applicant's ability to work is only partly visible. An examiner, or a judge on appeal, decides from the medical record. Those allowed rarely work again, partly because they cannot and partly because work would cost them the benefit. Those denied: some go back to work, some cannot. Errors go both ways, and both are costly. The key question is about the applicants on the margin, the ones an examiner might allow or deny: how much would they work without benefits?

In 2013 Nicole Maestas, Kathleen Mullen and Alexander Strand found a natural experiment inside the system. Applications are assigned to examiners essentially at random, and examiners differ. On the Island, two hundred examiners see similar applicants, yet most allow between about a quarter and three quarters of the claims they see. Compare allowed with denied applicants directly, and benefits seem to cut work by 57 percentage points. But the allowed are sicker; they would have worked less anyway. Instead, use the examiner's leniency as an instrument: the answer is 35 points, close to the truth for applicants on the margin, 32. Assignment by chance turns a judge's temperament into an experiment.

The average hides a range. On the Island, benefits displace a lot of work for applicants with mild impairments and almost none for the most severe, who could not work anyway. Maestas, Mullen and Strand found the same pattern in American data: no effect for those with the most severe impairments, and up to fifty percentage points for those with the least. So disability insurance works well where impairments are clear and less well where they are not, and the design question is how to tell the two apart, or how to let people try work without losing their benefits.
EITC: Chapter eleven. Help for the working poor.

How do you help people with low incomes without discouraging the work that would raise them? In the late 1960s the United States ran experiments on Milton Friedman's idea of a negative income tax: a guaranteed income, withdrawn gradually as earnings rise. Four experiments ran between 1968 and 1982; the largest, in Seattle and Denver, enrolled about 4,800 families. In Philip Robins's summary, husbands worked about five percent fewer hours, wives about twenty percent fewer, and single mothers about thirteen percent fewer. The reason is built in: a guarantee pays people who do not work, and withdrawing it as earnings rise is a tax on every extra hour.

America chose a different design: the Earned Income Tax Credit, paid only to those who work. Here is the 2025 schedule for a single parent with three or more children. For the first 17,880 dollars of earnings, the credit adds forty-five cents to each dollar earned: a wage subsidy, a negative marginal tax rate. It then stays at its maximum, 8,046 dollars, and from 23,350 dollars it is withdrawn at about twenty-one cents per dollar, until it is gone at about 61,555 dollars. The withdrawal is a tax on extra work, but only for those already working; for someone deciding whether to work at all, the credit is pure reward.

Does it work? In 1996 Nada Eissa and Jeffrey Liebman compared single women with and without children, before and after the credit was expanded in 1986: the mothers' participation in the labour force rose, and those already working did not cut their hours. On the Island, single parents decide whether to work, weighing earnings, the credit and the cost of a job against a welfare benefit. A credit ten percent larger draws in 1.2 percent more parents. Those new workers pay payroll tax and stop drawing welfare, so about 5 cents of each dollar comes back. Each net dollar spent delivers 1.06 dollars of value: a number that chapter thirteen puts on a common scale.

There is another way to avoid taxing work: base help on something people cannot easily change. George Akerlof called it tagging in 1978. On the Island a fifth of people are needy. A payment to everyone sends only a fifth of each dollar to them. A tag, such as a disability, young children or old age, catches seventy percent of the needy and ten percent of the rest. Pay only the tagged, and 64 percent of each dollar reaches the needy, and because the tag cannot be earned by working less, it does not discourage work. The price: 30 percent of the needy have no tag and get nothing. Every targeted programme makes this trade between reaching the needy and leaving some out.
UBI: A basic income pays everyone the same amount, with no conditions. What would it cost? The simplest version needs no new arithmetic: tax all income at a flat rate and pay the proceeds back equally. On the Island, with incomes around fifty thousand dollars, a thirty percent tax pays everyone 19,278 dollars a year. Everyone with an income below the average, 64,259 dollars, gains: 64 percent of people, because the average is above the typical income. The bottom tenth gains about fifteen thousand dollars, the top tenth pays about thirty-five. The Gini index falls from 0.38 to 0.27. It is the flat tax and equal transfer of Part forty, on a larger scale.

But taxes change what people earn. If no one responded, the basic income would rise in step with the tax rate. With an elasticity of taxable income of a quarter, as in Part forty-one, incomes shrink as the rate rises, so a thirty percent tax pays 17,633 dollars instead of 19,278. And there is a ceiling: the most the Island can pay is about 34,378 dollars, at a tax rate of 80 percent, the top of its Laffer curve. In a real budget the basic income would also compete with everything else the taxes pay for.

What do people do with unconditional money? Finland gave two thousand unemployed people five hundred and sixty euros a month for two years, without conditions: they worked slightly more than a control group and reported better wellbeing, though the survey had no baseline. In America, a study led by Eva Vivalt gave a thousand people a thousand dollars a month for three years: they worked about 1.3 hours a week less, a moderate effect, and spent more on basic needs. In rural Kenya, a study by Abhijit Banerjee, Tavneet Suri and coauthors found that lump sums did at least as well as the same money paid monthly, with no sign that the payments discouraged work. But a trial of a thousand people cannot show what happens when everyone receives the money and everyone pays the tax for it: prices, wages and the budget all change.
MVPF: This part has met pensions, unemployment benefits, health insurance, disability insurance and tax credits. How can they be compared? In 2020 Nathaniel Hendren and Ben Sprung-Keyser proposed one yardstick, the marginal value of public funds. For a small expansion of a policy, divide what its beneficiaries would be willing to pay for it by its net cost to the government. The net cost counts the policy's effects on the rest of the budget: taxes it brings back when people work or earn more, and other spending it causes or saves. Above one, each net dollar delivers more than a dollar of value. Below one, some of each dollar leaks away in changed behaviour. And if the policy raises more in later taxes than it costs, the value is infinite: it pays for itself.

On the Island, compute the value of a little more unemployment insurance at each benefit level. At a fifth of the wage, a little more is worth 1.27 dollars per net dollar, because the consumption it protects is valuable. At half the wage, only 0.66, because longer unemployment eats into the budget. At the best benefit of chapter two, exactly one: the Baily-Chetty formula is the condition that the last dollar is worth a dollar. The Island's earned income tax credit scores 1.06, because the parents it draws into work pay taxes and leave welfare. Now programmes as different as these can be ranked: spend the next dollar where the value per dollar is highest.

Hendren and Sprung-Keyser applied the yardstick to 133 American policies from the past half century. Most policies for adults, from unemployment insurance to tax credits and job training, scored between about a half and two. The highest scores went to health and education policies for children, and some of them paid for themselves: the children grew up to earn more and pay more tax than the programmes cost. The yardstick also links back to Part forty-one. Raising a dollar of tax costs taxpayers more than a dollar; a policy is worth paying for with a tax when its value per dollar beats the tax's. That is how the two sides of the budget meet.
Practice: Chapter fifteen. In practice: actuaries and evaluators.

Who does this for a living? Actuaries project a programme's income and costs far ahead; Social Security's Office of the Chief Actuary looks seventy-five years out, every year. Budget offices, like the Congressional Budget Office, score proposals to change benefits. State agencies run unemployment insurance, and set each employer's tax by its record of layoffs, so that firms that lay off more pay more. Evaluators, in government and universities, test programmes before they spread, as RAND and Oregon did. And insurers' actuaries price the private cover that sits alongside the state's.

Here is the kind of arithmetic an actuary does, with chapter eight's identity. Today, with 2.7 workers per beneficiary, a 12.4 percent payroll tax pays 33 percent of the average wage. If there are 2.3 workers per beneficiary in 2035 and the benefit is to stay the same, the tax must rise to 14.6 percent. If the tax is to stay the same, the benefit falls to 29 percent of the wage. Or some of each, or more workers: a later retirement age, more immigrants, higher employment. The arithmetic does not choose; it only says that something must give.

Called it? In 1983, with the trust funds months from running short, Congress raised payroll taxes sooner, taxed some benefits and raised the retirement age in steps. The reform was expected to keep Social Security solvent for seventy-five years, with surpluses in the early years paying for deficits later. Seventy-five years from 1983 is 2058. The trustees and the Congressional Budget Office now expect the trust funds to run out in 2034, about a quarter of a century early. The actuaries had expected annual deficits to begin around 2025; the economy and the population turned out differently from their assumptions. The verdict: wrong. Seventy-five-year promises depend on numbers no one can know so far ahead, which is why the actuaries re-run them every year.
